name: Langley Castle

tagline: 'Possibly the finest tower house in Northumberland,' burned by Henry IV's forces in 1405, ruined for centuries, then restored twice — first by Victorian historians, then into today's Grade I listed hotel
highlights: Built in 1350 by Sir Thomas de Lucy on a site that had been the 12th-century seat of the Barons of Tynedale — a four-storey H-plan tower house
Severely damaged in 1405 when forces loyal to Henry IV attacked the Percy family of Northumberland; left ruined for centuries afterward
Purchased in 1882 by Cadwallader Bates, who restored it with his wife Josephine — the hotel's Josephine Restaurant is named for her
Used as army barracks during the Second World War and later as a girls' school
Bought in 1986 by Stuart Madnick and converted into a hotel; Grade I listed and described by English Heritage as 'possibly the finest tower house in Northumberland'
description:
Langley Castle stands near Hexham in Northumberland, on a site whose fortified history reaches back to the 12th century, when it served as the seat of the Barons of Tynedale — a title connected to the border lordships that governed this contested stretch of country between England and Scotland. The castle in its current recognisable form was built in 1350 by Sir Thomas de Lucy, who raised a substantial four-storey tower house on an H-plan, a layout distinct from the more common rectangular or L-plan towers found elsewhere in the Anglo-Scottish Border region, giving Langley a genuinely distinctive architectural footprint among England's northern fortifications.

The castle's early history included genuine violence typical of this frontier landscape. In 1405, Langley was severely damaged during an attack by forces loyal to King Henry IV against the powerful Percy family of Northumberland, whose rebellion against the crown was one of the defining conflicts of the early 15th century. The damage inflicted in 1405 left Langley in a ruined state for centuries afterward, a fate shared by many Border fortifications that lost their strategic or family significance following the political realignments of the late medieval and early modern periods.

Langley's rescue from ruin came in 1882, when it was purchased by Cadwallader Bates, an antiquarian and local historian who undertook its restoration alongside his wife, Josephine. The couple's restoration returned Langley to habitable condition after roughly four and a half centuries of decay, and Josephine's name lives on today in the hotel's Josephine Restaurant, a direct and personal link between the Victorian-era restoration and the castle's present hospitality identity.

The 20th century brought further institutional uses typical of large historic buildings during this period: Langley served as army barracks during the Second World War, and subsequently operated as a girls' school before eventually being sold. Stuart Madnick purchased the castle in 1986 and converted it into the hotel that operates today. Langley holds Grade I listed status, the highest tier of architectural and historic building protection in England, and English Heritage has described it as possibly the finest tower house in the whole of Northumberland — a striking endorsement for a county with no shortage of significant fortified architecture, including Alnwick and Bamburgh castles within the same region.

Today's Langley Castle welcomes both hotel guests and non-residents to the Josephine Restaurant, which carries 2 AA Rosettes and offers a Table d'Hôte menu at £44.95 alongside a tasting menu from £65, plus the Drawing Room for afternoon tea and the more contemporary Glass Pavilion as an additional dining space. For visitors exploring Hadrian's Wall, Hexham Abbey or the wider Northumberland National Park, Langley offers a way to dine inside a genuinely significant medieval tower house without booking a room — a rare combination of a working Border fortress, a documented Victorian rescue story, and a modern, accessible dining offer built around English Heritage's own assessment of the building's singular architectural quality.

Langley's H-plan layout is itself worth understanding for visitors unfamiliar with medieval Border tower architecture: two projecting wings extend from a central block, an arrangement that gave defenders clearer sightlines along more of the building's perimeter than a simple rectangular tower could offer. Combined with walls several feet thick throughout, this design reflects the genuinely serious defensive requirements of a family building in Tynedale in the mid-14th century, a period when Border raiding and cross-frontier conflict were a routine feature of life in this part of Northumberland rather than an occasional disruption.
history: The site of Langley Castle had been the seat of the Barons of Tynedale since the 12th century. The current four-storey H-plan tower house was built in 1350 by Sir Thomas de Lucy. In 1405, the castle was severely damaged during an attack by forces loyal to Henry IV against the Percy family of Northumberland, and it remained ruined for centuries afterward. Cadwallader Bates purchased the castle in 1882 and restored it with his wife Josephine. Langley served as army barracks during the Second World War and later as a girls' school, before Stuart Madnick bought it in 1986 and converted it into a hotel. It holds Grade I listed status, and English Heritage has described it as possibly the finest tower house in Northumberland.

faqs.question: Can I eat at Langley Castle without staying overnight?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Josephine Restaurant, which carries 2 AA Rosettes, welcomes both hotel guests and non-residents, offering a Table d'Hôte menu at £44.95 and a tasting menu from £65. The Drawing Room serves afternoon tea, and the Glass Pavilion offers an additional, more contemporary dining space.

faqs.question: Why is the restaurant at Langley Castle called 'Josephine'?
faqs.answer: The Josephine Restaurant is named for Josephine Bates, who restored the ruined castle alongside her husband, Cadwallader Bates, after he purchased the property in 1882. Their restoration rescued Langley from roughly 450 years of decay following the severe damage it suffered in 1405.

faqs.question: What happened to Langley Castle in 1405?
faqs.answer: In 1405, Langley Castle was severely damaged during an attack by forces loyal to King Henry IV against the Percy family of Northumberland, whose rebellion against the crown was one of the major conflicts of the early 15th century. The castle remained in a ruined state for centuries until its restoration began in 1882.

faqs.question: What does 'H-plan' mean for a tower house like Langley Castle?
faqs.answer: An H-plan tower house has two wings projecting from a central block, resembling the letter H in floor plan. This gave defenders clearer sightlines along more of the building's perimeter than a simple rectangular tower, reflecting the genuinely serious defensive needs of a family building in Tynedale in the mid-14th century, when Border raiding was a routine feature of life in this part of Northumberland.
